questions.q: What is the relationship between a container IMAGE and a CONTAINER?
choices: A container is a running (or stopped) instance of an image
An image is a running container
An image is a VM snapshot
questions.explain: The image is the read-only template (layers). Running it creates a container with a thin writable layer on top. One image can spawn many containers.

questions.q: What does the FROM instruction in a Dockerfile do?
choices: Sets the base image the new image builds on
questions.explain: Every Dockerfile starts with FROM (e.g. `FROM python:3.12-slim`). Then RUN, COPY, ENV, EXPOSE, CMD/ENTRYPOINT build on top.

questions.q: What does EXPOSE 8080 in a Dockerfile actually do?
choices: Documents that the app listens on 8080; you still publish it with -p at run time
Opens port 8080 on the host firewall
questions.explain: EXPOSE is metadata. Use `docker run -p 8080:8080` (host:container) to actually publish the port.

questions.q: What's the key difference between containers and virtual machines?
choices: Containers share the host OS kernel; VMs each run a full guest OS on a hypervisor
Containers need a hypervisor; VMs don't
questions.explain: Sharing the kernel makes containers lightweight (MBs, start in seconds). VMs offer stronger isolation and can run different OSes.

questions.q: What is the smallest deployable unit in Kubernetes?
questions.explain: A Pod wraps one or more containers that share a network namespace (one IP) and storage volumes.

questions.q: What does a Kubernetes Deployment do?
choices: Maintains a desired number of identical pod replicas and manages rolling updates
Exposes pods on a stable IP
questions.explain: Deployment → ReplicaSet → Pods. Change the image and it rolls out new pods gradually; `kubectl rollout undo` rolls back.

questions.q: Pods come and go with changing IPs. What gives clients a stable virtual IP and DNS name for a set of pods?
questions.explain: A Service selects pods by label and load-balances across them. Types: ClusterIP (internal), NodePort, LoadBalancer.

questions.q: Which Service type opens the same high port (30000–32767 by default) on every node?
questions.explain: NodePort exposes the service on each node's IP. LoadBalancer builds on it by asking the cloud for an external load balancer.

questions.q: Where should a database password go in Kubernetes?
questions.explain: Secrets are for sensitive data; ConfigMaps for plain config. Note that Secrets are only base64-encoded by default, so enable encryption at rest and lock down RBAC.

questions.q: What is a Kubernetes Namespace for?
choices: Logically separating resources (teams, environments) within one cluster
questions.explain: Namespaces scope names, RBAC and resource quotas. e.g. `dev`, `staging`, `prod` or one per team.

questions.q: A pod shows status CrashLoopBackOff. What does that mean?
choices: The container keeps crashing after start, and Kubernetes waits longer between each restart
The node is out of disk
The pod is waiting for a volume
questions.explain: The app starts then exits. Run `kubectl logs <pod> --previous` to see why it died. ImagePullBackOff, by contrast, means the image can't be pulled.

questions.q: What does `kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml` do?
choices: Creates or updates resources to match the manifest (declarative)
questions.explain: You declare desired state in YAML and Kubernetes reconciles reality to match. Apply the same file twice and nothing changes: idempotent!

questions.q: What language are Terraform configurations written in?
questions.explain: HCL files end in .tf. Providers (AWS, Azure, GCP, even Cisco and Palo Alto) translate resources into API calls.

questions.q: What does `terraform plan` do?
choices: Shows what changes would be made, without making them
questions.explain: Always read the plan: + create, ~ update in place, -/+ replace, - destroy. `terraform apply` executes it.

questions.q: What is the Terraform state file for?
choices: It maps your configuration to the real resources Terraform manages
It's a log of past runs
questions.explain: Without state, Terraform can't know what it created. Teams store it remotely (S3 + locking, Terraform Cloud) so two people don't apply at once. It can contain secrets: protect it!

questions.q: Which is a key benefit of Infrastructure as Code?
choices: Infrastructure is version-controlled, reviewable and reproducible
It removes the need for any testing
It makes clicking in consoles faster
questions.explain: IaC brings software practices (Git, PRs, CI) to infrastructure. Rebuild an environment identically from code, and know exactly what changed and when.

questions.q: What does 'declarative' mean for tools like Terraform and Kubernetes?
choices: You describe the desired end state; the tool works out the steps
You list every step in order
You must write it in Python
questions.explain: Declarative: 'there should be 3 web servers'. Imperative: 'create a server, then another, then another'. Declarative tools converge on the desired state.

questions.q: Renting raw virtual machines, storage and networks that YOU manage the OS on is:
questions.explain: IaaS = you manage OS and up (EC2, Azure VMs). PaaS = you bring code; the platform runs it. SaaS = finished app (Gmail, Microsoft 365). FaaS = serverless functions.

questions.q: Webmail like Gmail or Outlook.com is an example of:
questions.explain: Software as a Service: you just use the application; the provider manages everything underneath.

questions.q: What makes a subnet 'public' in an AWS VPC?
choices: Its route table has a default route to an Internet Gateway
It uses public IP ranges in its CIDR
questions.explain: Public subnet = 0.0.0.0/0 → IGW. Instances also need a public IP (or Elastic IP) to be reachable from the internet.

questions.q: Instances in a PRIVATE subnet need to download OS updates from the internet without being reachable from it. What do you use?
choices: A NAT gateway in a public subnet
An internet gateway attached to the private subnet
A public IP on each instance
questions.explain: The private subnet's default route points at a NAT gateway, which does PAT outbound. Unsolicited inbound connections can't get in.

questions.q: Security groups vs network ACLs in AWS: which statement is correct?
choices: Security groups are stateful and per-instance; NACLs are stateless and per-subnet
Security groups are stateless; NACLs are stateful
NACLs attach to instances; security groups attach to subnets
questions.explain: SGs track connections (return traffic auto-allowed, allow rules only). NACLs are stateless (you must allow return traffic, including ephemeral ports), support deny rules, and are evaluated in rule order.

questions.q: What is a VPC (Virtual Private Cloud)?
choices: A logically isolated virtual network you define inside a public cloud
questions.explain: You pick its CIDR (e.g. 10.0.0.0/16), carve subnets across availability zones and control routing and security. Yes, subnetting skills matter in the cloud!

questions.q: What is an Availability Zone?
choices: One or more isolated data centers within a region, with independent power and networking
A country where the cloud is legal
questions.explain: Spread resources across multiple AZs for high availability. If one AZ fails, the others keep serving.

questions.q: Adding MORE instances behind a load balancer to handle load is:
questions.explain: Horizontal = more machines. Vertical = a bigger machine (more CPU/RAM). Cloud-native apps prefer horizontal: it's elastic and avoids a single point of failure.

questions.q: A container exits with code 137 and Kubernetes says OOMKilled. What happened?
choices: It exceeded its memory limit and the kernel killed it (SIGKILL = 128 + 9)
questions.explain: Exit code 137 = 128 + signal 9. Raise the memory limit, or fix the leak (hello, Memory Leak Slime).

questions.q: What is a container registry?
choices: A service that stores and distributes container images (Docker Hub, ECR, GHCR)
questions.explain: CI builds an image, pushes it to a registry, and clusters pull it from there. Pin specific tags or digests rather than :latest in production.

questions.q: What is Docker Compose used for?
choices: Defining and running multi-container apps from one YAML file
questions.explain: compose.yaml describes services, networks and volumes. `docker compose up -d` starts the whole stack. Great for labs, like a containerized network lab!

questions.q: What does a Kubernetes Ingress provide?
choices: HTTP(S) routing from outside the cluster to Services based on host/path rules
questions.explain: An Ingress controller (e.g. NGINX) reads Ingress rules like 'api.netrealm.io/v1 → api-service'. It handles TLS termination too.

questions.q: An organization runs some workloads in its own data center and some in a public cloud, connected together. This is:
questions.explain: Hybrid = on-prem + public cloud integrated (often via VPN or a dedicated link like Direct Connect). Multicloud = using several public clouds.

questions.q: Running code as functions triggered by events, with no servers to manage, is called:
questions.explain: AWS Lambda, Azure Functions, Cloud Run functions. You pay per invocation; the provider handles scaling. (There are still servers, just not yours.)

questions.q: What happens when a container fails its LIVENESS probe?
choices: The pod is removed from Service endpoints but not restarted
questions.explain: Liveness failure → restart. READINESS failure → stop sending traffic (removed from endpoints) until it's ready again.

questions.q: List the RUNNING containers on this Docker host.
questions.output:
CONTAINER ID   IMAGE          STATUS         PORTS                  NAMES
3f2a9c1d8e7b   nginx:1.27     Up 2 hours     0.0.0.0:8080->80/tcp   web
9b1c2d3e4f5a   redis:7        Up 2 hours     6379/tcp               cache
questions.explain: `docker ps` shows running containers; `docker ps -a` includes stopped ones.

questions.q: Build an image from the Dockerfile in the current directory and tag it netapp:1.0
questions.output:
[+] Building 14.2s (9/9) FINISHED
 => [1/4] FROM docker.io/library/python:3.12-slim
 => [4/4] RUN pip install -r requirements.txt
 => naming to docker.io/library/netapp:1.0
questions.explain: The final `.` is the build context (the files sent to the builder). `-t` names and tags the image.

questions.q: Run nginx in the background (detached), publishing host port 8080 to container port 80.
questions.explain: `-d` = detached, `-p 8080:80` = HOST:CONTAINER. Browse to http://localhost:8080 to reach nginx on port 80 inside.

questions.q: Show the logs of the container named web.
questions.explain: `docker logs web` (add `-f` to follow). Containers should log to stdout/stderr so the platform can collect the logs.

questions.q: List the pods in the current namespace.
questions.output:
NAME                   READY   STATUS             RESTARTS      AGE
web-7d4f9c8b6-2xkqz    1/1     Running            0             3h
web-7d4f9c8b6-9hmtp    1/1     Running            0             3h
api-5c6b7d8f9-lq2wd    0/1     CrashLoopBackOff   7 (2m ago)    25m
questions.explain: `kubectl get pods` (or `po`). Add `-o wide` for node and pod IP, `-A` for all namespaces. Spot the CrashLoopBackOff!

questions.q: Show detailed info and recent EVENTS for the pod api-5c6b7d8f9-lq2wd.
questions.output:
Name:         api-5c6b7d8f9-lq2wd
Status:       Running
    Last State:     Terminated
      Reason:       Error
      Exit Code:    1
Events:
  Warning  BackOff  2m (x31 over 25m)  kubelet  Back-off restarting failed container api
questions.explain: `kubectl describe` shows config, container state, exit codes and the Events list: the first stop for scheduling, image-pull and probe failures.

questions.q: Show the application logs from the pod api-5c6b7d8f9-lq2wd.
questions.output:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/app/main.py", line 12, in <module>
    db = connect(os.environ["DB_HOST"])
KeyError: 'DB_HOST'
questions.explain: `kubectl logs <pod>` (add `--previous` for the crashed instance). Here the root cause is a missing DB_HOST environment variable!

questions.q: Apply the manifest file deployment.yaml to the cluster.
questions.explain: Declarative: 'configured' means it updated an existing object to match the file; 'created' means it was new; 'unchanged' means nothing to do.

questions.q: Scale the deployment named web to 3 replicas.
questions.explain: Imperative scaling works, but the next `kubectl apply` of the YAML will reset it. Prefer changing `replicas:` in Git, or use a HorizontalPodAutoscaler.

questions.q: Initialize this Terraform working directory (download providers, set up the backend).
questions.output:
Initializing the backend...
Initializing provider plugins...
- Installing hashicorp/aws v5.80.0...
Terraform has been successfully initialized!
questions.explain: `terraform init` is always the first command in a new or cloned config. Re-run it after adding providers or modules.

questions.q: Preview the changes Terraform would make, without applying them.
questions.explain: Read every plan carefully, especially lines with `-` (destroy) or `-/+` (replace). In CI, save it with `-out=plan.tfplan` and apply exactly that plan.

questions.q: Apply the Terraform changes to create the infrastructure.
questions.output:
aws_subnet.private_b: Creating...
aws_subnet.private_b: Creation complete after 1s [id=subnet-0a1b2c3d]
Apply complete! Resources: 1 added, 0 changed, 0 destroyed.
questions.explain: `terraform apply` shows the plan and asks for confirmation (unless you give it a saved plan or -auto-approve). State is updated afterwards.

questions.q: List the container images stored locally.
questions.output:
REPOSITORY   TAG       IMAGE ID       CREATED        SIZE
netapp       1.0       a1b2c3d4e5f6   5 minutes ago  142MB
nginx        1.27      7f553e8bbc89   3 weeks ago    192MB
questions.explain: `docker images` (or `docker image ls`). Clean up unused images with `docker image prune`.

questions.q: Open an interactive shell (sh) inside the running container named web.
questions.explain: `docker exec -it` runs a new process in an existing container: -i keeps stdin open, -t allocates a TTY. The Kubernetes equivalent is `kubectl exec -it <pod> -- sh`.

questions.q: Order the core Terraform workflow.
questions.explain: Write → init (providers/backend) → plan (preview) → apply (execute). `terraform destroy` tears it all down when you're finished.

questions.q: Order the typical container delivery workflow.
items: Pull and run it on the target (docker run / Kubernetes)
questions.explain: In CI/CD, the build and push happen in the pipeline; Kubernetes pulls the image when the Deployment is updated.

questions.q: Order the hops for an external HTTPS request reaching an app in Kubernetes.
questions.explain: LB → Ingress controller (host/path routing, TLS) → Service (stable VIP, load balancing) → a Pod's IP → the app listening inside the container.

questions.q: What is the name of the Kubernetes command-line tool?
questions.explain: kubectl, pronounced 'kube-control', 'kube-cuttle' or 'kube-C-T-L'. Engineers will argue about it forever.

questions.q: Which Dockerfile instruction sets the base image?
questions.explain: FROM. Multi-stage builds use several FROM lines to keep the final image small.

questions.q: What file extension do Terraform configuration files use?
questions.explain: .tf (plus .tfvars for variable values). State lives in terraform.tfstate, which should NOT be committed to Git.

questions.q: Your VPC is 10.0.0.0/16. Which subnet CIDR could you create INSIDE it?
questions.explain: Subnets must fall inside the VPC range: 10.0.0.0–10.0.255.255. 10.0.0.0/8 is bigger than the VPC; the others are outside it.
